text: Disaster recovery for AI infrastructure uses the same discipline you already know from earlier in this path — define an RTO and an RPO, then build backup, replication, and failover to meet them. What changes is the asset list. Model artifacts, the trained weights actually deployed to serve predictions, and training checkpoints, the intermediate saves during a long run, are exactly as critical as a production database, and exactly as capable of being lost permanently if nobody treats them that way.

Not every artifact deserves the same backup policy. The production model registry rarely changes, so replicating it synchronously or near-synchronously to a secondary region is cheap relative to the cost of losing it — an outage with no known-good model to fail back to. Training checkpoints can tolerate a larger RPO, because losing the most recent one costs something bounded and known: the GPU-hours since the last successful save, not an indefinite loss. That's a real business tradeoff, not a default setting.

A traditional DR plan for a stateless service assumes the secondary region can simply provide equivalent compute the moment you fail over. That assumption breaks for GPU-backed workloads. The failover region might not have the GPU SKU you need sitting available, even though networking, data replication, and DNS all work perfectly. A DR plan that doesn't explicitly address this isn't complete — it works right up until the moment it needs capacity that isn't there.

Address it with the same tools from the capacity planning lesson, applied to DR specifically: hold a standing capacity reservation in the failover region sized for your DR scenario, or define an explicit, pre-approved degraded mode — a smaller model, a CPU-only serving path, reduced request volume — that the plan falls back to. Deciding this inside the written plan, instead of improvising it during an actual incident, is what keeps a DR exercise from turning into a prolonged outage.

A DR plan that's never exercised is a guess. Test restoring a model from its replica and confirming it actually serves correct predictions, not just that the file copied. Test resuming a training run from its most recent checkpoint. And test failing inference traffic over to reserved or degraded-mode capacity, confirming it serves traffic within the latency SLOs from the previous lesson. That closes the chapter: capacity planning, regional strategy, SLOs, and disaster recovery all working together for AI infrastructure that actually survives contact with reality.
